There has been a broad inquiry over the past several years into reproducibility, though.

http://www.nature.com/news/1-500-scientists-lift-the-lid-on-reproducibility-1.19970

I think the most illustrative thing about this fMRI case is that even trained or respectable scientists don't have the time or skills necessary to validate what software is doing for them. I have worked with a lot of biologists and neuroscientists, and most of them do not develop an understanding of the algorithms being used by tools that they employ. Therefore, they can't imagine what could go wrong, and they also don't have the computer science or statistics know-how to conduct side experiments or sanity checks which will validate their results. Basically, the "validation" loop often looks something like this:

Some bio/CS folks create a tool => they publish a rough description of how it works along with pictures or results that look compelling => others start using the tool and publishing results that seem intuitive => the tool gains reputation based on popularity and becomes a "standard"

I think for the most part these tools are well designed by smart well intentioned people, but this fMRI case illustrates how error-prone this way of conducting science is.

I personally would love to be a science "QA" type person-- digging through other people's work and trying to find gross faults. There is just not much money in it though, at least not yet.
